1.explanation: • rules/prefer-const.md: Documents how the “prefer-const” rule’s fixer transforms `let` to `const` and under which conditions. • rules/no-undef-init.md: Explains the “no-undef-init” rule’s logic and its fixer (which removes `= undefined`). • developer-guide/working-with-rules.md: Shows how rules are implemented and registered, including how fixers are defined. • developer-guide/code-path-analysis.md: Describes the code-path and fix application ordering in ESLint’s core, key to understanding why one fix overrides another. • developer-guide/source-code.md: Guides you to the actual source code locations for ESLint rules and the fixer engine, so you can locate and modify the implementation. • developer-guide/architecture.md: Provides a high-level view of ESLint’s architecture, including the sequence of rule execution and autofix application, which is crucial to reproducing and fixing the issue.
1.bug_scenario: In this scenario, the developer has a simple JavaScript file (testfile.js) containing a single declaration: “let teste = undefined;”. They are using ESLint v6.8.0 with the default parser and a configuration that enables two rules: “prefer-const” (error) and “no-undef-init” (warn). In their .eslintrc.js they’ve set these rules, expecting  ESLint’s autofix (`eslint --fix`) to convert the declaration to `const teste = undefined;` or to leave the initialization in place. Instead, what actually happens is that eslint first applies the “prefer-const” fix (converting `let` to `const`) and then the “no-undef-init” fix (removing the initialization of `undefined`), resulting in `const teste;`. This leads to a syntax error at runtime because JavaScript does not allow an uninitialized const. The screenshot shows VSCode with the source file on the left, the .eslintrc.js on the right, and a terminal at the bottom where the eslint command was run. The buggy behavior is due to the order in which autofixes are applied, causing conflicting transformations.
